title: Fifty thousand years
hookLine: the angels and the Spirit ascend in a day of fifty thousand years (70:4)

lines: A DAY ISN'T ALWAYS A DAY.
cards: Waiting rooms do strange things to time. Ten minutes at the dentist can feel like an hour; an hour with someone you love disappears like ten minutes.
A childhood summer can feel endless; a grown-up summer can be gone before the sunscreen is bought. A day isn't always a day.
Surah al-Ma'arij, the Ascending Stairways, opens with a number that stretches that feeling as far as it can go: a day whose measure is fifty thousand years.

teach.h: THE LORD OF THE ASCENDING WAYS.
teach.b: The surah is named for verse three: Allah is Dhu al-Ma'arij, the Lord of the ascending stairways, the ways up. Then verse four: the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years.

teach.h: WHO IS THE SPIRIT? SOME SAY JIBRIL.
teach.b: Some commentators say Jibril, the angel of revelation, named separately here for his rank; others say a different creation. The verse doesn't say. And what is the day?
Some say it's the Day of Judgment, which will feel that long to those who face it, and the surah does go straight on to describe that day: the sky like molten metal, mountains like tufts of wool.
Others say it's the distance of the ascent itself, a journey that would take a human fifty thousand years.
And a hadith in Sahih Muslim, about those who never paid the zakat on their wealth, speaks of a day whose length is fifty thousand years. Now set this beside two other verses.
In surah as-Sajdah, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of your counting; in surah al-Hajj, the same.

teach.h: A THOUSAND HERE, FIFTY THOUSAND THERE.
teach.b: A thousand here, fifty thousand there. Scholars explain the difference in different ways, and the common thread they draw is that Allah's days aren't measured by our clocks. Our impatience runs on hours.

teach.h: THEY SEE IT FAR, WE SEE IT NEAR.
teach.b: In verse five the surah asks for sabr jamil, beautiful patience, and verses six and seven add: they see the day as far off, and We see it near.

how: Commentators read 70:4 alongside 32:5 and 22:47 as teaching that Allah's time is not measured like human time; commentators differ on whether the fifty-thousand-year day is the Day of Judgment or the span of the angels' ascent.

o: beautiful patience, what the surah asks for
a long, beautiful day spent near God
a beautiful reward promised to those who wait

games.q: you notice one verse says a thousand years and another fifty thousand. what common thread do scholars draw?
o: one verse is a copying error.
Allah's days aren't measured by our clocks.
the numbers are about the calendar.
games.why: scholars explain the difference in various ways; the common ground is that Allah's time isn't ours. they see it far, We see it near.

practice: Close your eyes and count your breaths slowly, noticing how long one breath really is when you're doing nothing else, and the gap before the next one.
Somewhere in that stillness, hold something you've been impatient about inside this slower time, and see whether it looks any different.

wordCard.voice: Sabr jamil, beautiful patience: what the surah asks for, since a day with Allah is not measured by our clocks. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the ascending stairways, the ways up; Allah is Dhu al-Ma'arij, Lord of them (70:3).

carryVoice: Your line: his day is long. What feels far may be near. That's day six hundred forty-five.
